And for anyone who laughs or smiles, I will recite why I do not have confidence. I do not intend to take too long but I go back, as other hon. members have done, to this whole problem of insurrection, of terrorism, of revolution, and of the FLQ. It did not come about last Thursday. It came six or seven years ago when the first bomb exploded and injured or killed, I forget which, someone. That was when the FLQ was born. If it had not been the FLQ as such it might have been some other organization because, at the moment, the world is full of revolutionary organizations. But what happened?
In October, 1969, Mr. Saulnier, the same man who wrote the letter that was supposed to be one of the catalysts for the Prime Minister's decision to invoke the War Measures Act, wrote the Prime Minister. When the Prime Minister was asked about this letter, because it was produced at a committee meeting, he had paid so little attention to it that he did not remember receiving it. This was the letter indicating there ought to be a security commission to investigate what was going on in Montreal. To his credit, and to the credit of his advisers, he was informed before the day was out that his answer was wrong. He came back into the House and apologized.
But, Mr. Speaker, this was a letter from Mr. Saulnier, from an important individual to an important individual about an important subject, and I found it difficult to appreciate fully the memory lapse the Prime Minister had.
You, Mr. Speaker, and all other members of the House know that after that letter was sent other events occurred. Just about a year ago, close to Hallowe'en
night, there was the Montreal police strike. There were fires in the city of Montreal, and a policeman was killed. Other events occurred that brought a parliamentary committee into being to investigate the CYC. The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert has reviewed all that for us. Earlier today the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) gave some evidence of his attempts to attract the attention of the government to some affairs going on in Montreal as far back as 1963. Then, there was Expo '67 when the Cuban embassy or pavilion was allegedly giving out pamphlets dealing with terrorism revolution and insurrection. But nothing was done.
As a member of the committee that investigated the Company of Young Canadians, the committee to which Mr. Saulnier and Mr. Drapeau gave evidence, I well remember that from some of the press, and certainly from the majority of the members of this House, came the allegation that we were witch hunting. Government members indulged in white-washing, trying to cover their own administrative mistakes and to point the finger at somebody else. That left things up in the air, and the request for a security commission went unheeded. That is point No. 2.
Now, I come down to a political area where I would expect that the judgment of the Prime Minister, and of the members of his party from Quebec, would be far superior to mine. It was only about a month and a half before the provincial election in Quebec that the Prime Minister said certain things, in that colourful phraseology that he uses. He said that the Parti Quebecois had miniscule support in Quebec. He used other objectives about the people who supported that party, all of which gave me the impression that it was a pretty small unit and that the election would take care of it.

I say the election did not take care of the problem in Quebec or in Canada, and the problem in Canada vis-a-vis Quebec will not be taken care of as long as the Prime Minister tries to use, as a dose of castor oil for the terrorists, those constitutional policies he is applying unilaterally across Canada. We are all a little different in the different parts of Canada. The hon. member for Coast-Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) and I who come from two different coasts are a little different. I say that difference stems from the collective way of life of the respective societies we have in the provinces.
After that I was a little perturbed at the Prime Minister's underestimation of the political support for this

October 17, 1970

separatist party. Then, when I was back in Nova Scotia, involved in some other events, I read in the newspaper that the Prime Minister had been talking about bleeding-hearts on Parliament Hill and weak-kneed legislators. I did not think that was quite the type of remark to make about a serious subject. What did not help me either was a picture on the front page of the Montreal Gazette the day after showing his bullet-proof 1 mousine, and his big fist sticking out of the window at the reporter's camera. Perhaps it was just one of his gestures, but when there had already been blood on the streets of Ottawa not to ment.on Montreal, it is no joke. My faith was shaken, but I was still prepared to give him the benefit of the doubt.
Then, the Prime Minister bawled out the press for giving free publicity to the FLQ. He asked, "What are you trying to do" or words to that effect, yet within 48 hours we had the War Measures Act introduced which gave the FLQ a status internationally that it never had previously. I am not going to go into what has happened since the proclamation was issued, but there are other matters that make me ponder about the judgment of the Prime Minister in these areas of his supposed expertise.
I could not understand why it was the Quebec Minister of Justice who answered to the world about the kidnapping of the diplomat, Mr. Cross. I though it should have been the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). But we all heard Mr. Cho-quette, and his very first words were, "I am instructed by the federal government to say..." This is a little thing, but the whole bundle bothers me, Mr. Speaker.
I come now to the use of the powers given by the War Measures Act. I do not know all these individuals in Quebec who have been arrested. I believe that in his statement the Prime Minister was kind enough to
Invoking of War Measures Act say he would come back to this House if that were done and lay the proclamation on the table for study. That does not leave me too satisfied.

That may be a sad commentary on our society. It is also sad that the one Canada in which many Canadians believe has become the armed Canada for many of us, that the just society has become the armed society and that the flower power of the Prime Minister has become soldier power around Parliament Hill. These are not all troubles of the Prime Minister's making. Expectations were raised, some have not been realized and the inevitable frustrations have set in. We must have conciliation and not confrontation in order to resolve conflicts between people.
The Prime Minister's Achilles heel is that he utilizes logic and textbooks in attempting to solve the problems of people. You cannot resolve problems with logic and textbooks alone; you must realize that the human element is also involved. That, I am afraid, is where the Prime Minister has overstepped the mark.
Some of the people, quite logically, stand behind the Prime Minister tonight in the implementation of the War Measures Act. But will they be behind him three months or six months from now, especially if we find out that there was no real basis for these stringent methods and that proper procedures in the police courts and jails have not been followed? Is it not a painful paradox that a man such as the Prime Minister, who thought the World War II was a war of imperialism, should now use the power of war to fight a perverted nationalism?

October 17, 1970
Invoking of War Measures Act
It is also a passing strange paradox that the discussion of the Bill of Rights and its underlying philosophy that was the highlight of a federal-provincial conference, should now have shifted, and that we should be debating a proclamation which gives the government almost absolute power over all of us. The government has panicked because of the actions of a few.
I listened with a great deal of interest, as I usually do, to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). I was appalled by some of his analogies, by some of his red herrings and the smokescreen he tried to lay. I was not appalled at his sincerity because I fully accept that. When he talked about our Prime Minister and his contribution to civil liberties in Quebec, I wanted to ask him whether in his heart of hearts he thought that if the powers under the War Measures Act had been invoked at the time of the asbestos strike, the Prime Minister would have ended up in jail.
I ask two questions about this measure. Is it right to invoke it? Will it succeed? Some tried to leave with us a pretty clear inference that underlying the all-encompassing powers under the War Measures Act which has been invoked is information that is available to members on the government side but is not available to members of other caucuses-the caucus I belong to, the NDP caucus and the Creditiste caucus. If that is so, it makes a mockery of our unity. That will not unify us.
[DOT] (11:30 p.m.)
Another question is this: Will the measure succeed? I put this question to all members of the House and especially to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). Has the knock at night, or has repression by day in any jurisdiction in the world solved the political problems of the society concerned? Such action might divert people's attention. It might put a damper on them. It might put them behind bars for awhile. One should take off one's blinkers and look around at the world to appreciate that people no longer want a strong father figure to govern them. The knock at night, whether at four o'clock or two o'clock, and continuing repression by day on the part of any government with unique powers will not resolve political problems. Such action will defeat their solution. After all, fear breeds fear and force answers force; and power without persuasion and belief is about as permanent as quicksand.
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, not because I want to alienate anyone but because there may be some in Quebec tonight who have supported the Parti Quebecois but who subsequently thought there was a federal option and were prepared to opt for it: these people may be alienated. Some people may have had friends in the FLQ; they may not have thought them such bad fellows. I am not talking about people like Vallieres; I am talking about some others. For instance, two good friends of mine went to see Chartrand speaking in Montreal. They were not very impressed by him. But by imprisoning some of these people are we not in danger of making martyrs of some and heroes of others?
Will not the task of those who like the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) opted for federalism be made more difficult? Unfortunately, I was not here to listen to the minister's speech but he, on behalf of the French-speaking Canadians he represents, opted for federalism. Will these repressive measures not confirm some of the misleading propaganda and literature that has been prostituted by the FLQ? That is what bothers me, Mr. Speaker.
I will spend little time answering the argument put forward by the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher). Some have asked whether the implementation of the War Measures Act is legal. There is no question but that the Prime Minister can quite legally invoke the War Measures Act, but that is not the test we should use. The test is whether it is right and whether it will work. There was a man in Munich who created legal tribunals and appointed judges to be the dispensers of justice meted out by those tribunals. He headed a parliament that passed laws and made certain people criminals. He was interviewed by a British correspondent, Sefton Delmer of the Daily Express, on March 3, 1933. I am referring to social history. These facts are contained in Alan Bullock's book, "Hitler, a study in tyranny".
Mr. Delmer made inquiries about certain powers that had been assumed after Hitler had asked for them following an unfortunate incident involving the burning of the Reichstag on February 27, 1933. I am not trying to suggest that anything like that is happening here. I am only trying to meet the argument that this action is legal, and therefore good. Because of the fact it is legal, it should be carefully scrutinized by every member. Look at the answer given to the correspondent, a member of the fourth estate, with reference to these changes in civil liberties. The correspondent from the Daily Express asked him what truth there was in rumours of a projected massacre of his political opponents Hitler replied:
My dear Delmar, I need no St. Bartholomew's Night. By the decrees issued legally we have appointed tribunals which will try enemies of the state legally, and deal with them legally in a way which will put an end to these conspiracies.
This interview with Hitler appeared in the Daily Express on March 3, 1933. I would like to put something else on the record with regard to legality. It is a statement of a politician, and it reads:
The streets of our country are in turmoil. The universities are filled with students rebelling and rioting. Communists are seeking to destroy our country. Russia is threatening us with her might and the republic is in danger. Yes, danger from within and without. We need law and order.
If I asked some people who said that, I might get the answer "Spiro Agnew". However, this is what Adolf Hitler said in 1932. This is the serious aspect of what we are debating here tonight. I am unalterably opposed to the War Measures Act being invoked at this time, unless the Prime Minister can take my leader or the members of Parliament into his confidence and tell us what happened in the last seven years that makes last Thursday any different from the six and a half years before that.

As far as the powers are concerned and the argument that they are only for six months with the option to renew I point out that in Greece, the foundation for the western democracy, a junta there some years ago passed extraordinary emergency powers on a temporary basis because of insurrection. I forget all the names, but that junta is still in command and these extraordinary emergency powers are still in operation. This happened in a country where they said it could not happen.
We should not be concerned about what is happening because of the soldiers on the streets and the bombs, but because of what Parliament is doing. We should look to the south where they have had selective assassination. They have had more bombings than Quebec and Montreal have had. Several years ago 40 blocks of the city of Chicago were burned. There were more blocks burned in the city of Los Angeles than in any city in this country. The government, be it state, congress or the president, have done nothing more than call out the national guard to put out the fires and to shoot the snipers. Have they taken away the civil liberties by due process of law? I say no.
When talking about the White Paper six months or a year ago, the Prime Minister and some ministers of the government smugly talked about the difference in social values between this country and the United States. If we move ahead with this War Measures Act for six months with an option to renew, no longer will a politician or any Canadian be able to stand smugly and suggest that social values in this country are far superior to those south of the border. With all their stress and strain, selective assassinations, bombings and killings, that country has not done what we propose to do on Monday when we vote on this.

In the years that I have been here there have only been four or five debates that have deserved the attention of all Members of Parliament in the way this debate has. I wish to comment on the calibre of the speeches that have been made. Most of the people I have listened to have been very sincere in the arguments they
Invoking of War Measures Act advanced. Very little time has been spent on defending the government's position, but rather they have spoken about the position of the individual and his role.
I was interested in the speech of the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau). He indicated that the Prime Minister has the support of most of the people in this country. He used the figure of 99 per cent. I do not think that is correct. We must discount the FLQ and their supporters. We must also discount other people for various reasons. These people believe that the Prime Minister has suddenly said "To hell with Quebec. We are putting the army in Quebec to straighten out these people. They are going to be just like other Canadians when I finish with them."

The people from Quebec, on the other hand, are saying that the army was put in to keep things the way they are. There are some very distinguished people in this House from Quebec, but they always refer to themselves as Quebeckers. I never refer to myself as an Ontarian. The only other people in this House who refer to themselves by a provincial name are the Newfoundlanders, but there may be others who use a fancy name. Sometimes the people from Alberta use the designation Albertan. Ever since I have been in this House, the people from Quebec have called themselves Quebeckers. Since I have been in this House people who have come here from Quebec have always said, "We are different. We want to run our own affairs. We do not want legislation passed nationally because it may hurt us provincially. We will not let you play a role."
The leaders we have had, with rare exceptions, have been provincial first, and then come to Ottawa for various reasons later. Most members will agree that in this debate many of the members from Quebec have considered their own situation. I do not blame them for this because the situation there is very bad. If the action of the Prime Minister is going to work, those cabinet ministers who are provincialists will have to give up some of the things that they think are essential to the province of Quebec. They must work to make it more like the other provinces. There must be a Canadian atmosphere rather than "What can we get and what can you do for us?". What they should be asking is, what they can do for the rest of Canada. Most members from other provinces have always been sympathetic toward Quebec.
Some speakers from the Liberal party have referred to the two party policy of the New Democratic Party. I agree that we have had that. The same people I am speaking of have advised us many times about the type of policy we should have. We listened to them because we did not know what was going on in the province of Quebec. We could not speak the language. The adherents to my party have been limited in Quebec. We were sold

October 17, 1970
Invoking of War Measures Act all kinds of ideas. People who have been in the party for a long time have sold us many ideas. It is very surprising tonight, but I am not unhappy to see, that one them is in gaol and the other one is in the Senate. These are people who have been giving us ideas from that province for many years. Maybe that is not the way they should end up. Some of those who have given us advice are in the cabinet today. I make no apology for the mistakes that we have made. We have made them with the best of intentions. We agreed to everything they asked for and they asked for various things over the years. We got ourselves into one hell of a position, and if you ask me what the policy of the New Democratic Party was for the Province of Quebec I haven't the faintest notion, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (11:40 p.m.)
I believe, however, that there are a lot of people in the Province of Quebec who do believe they should have the opportunity of participating. You can remember, Mr. Speaker, when we passed the Trans-Canada Highway Act and other acts-you can name them by the dozen-and Quebec said: Not us, don't run the highway through Quebec because it costs federal money. We got around to a state in which whatever was done for Quebec it could not be said the federal government had done it. For example, in the case of a technical school, we do not say that the federal government put up 75 per cent of the money. We only talk about the 25 per cent the Province puts up and we allow the Province total control. Rightly so, Mr. Speaker, because Quebec asked for it. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do not speak very loudly and I know how much you want to hear what I have to say. We heard the Prime Minister speak yesterday. I was quite impressed by his television appearance. He did a fine job. He mentioned how fragile our democratic system is, and how fine a line there is between stability and democracy. I agree with him. It takes a crisis of this magnitude for the government to realize that it must act. I believe one of the greatest blows democracy in this country received was when this government came to power.
First, this government whittled away at the democratic rights of Parliament during the last two years. Second, we have lost our civil rights completely for a period of six months with no real explanation concerning why such a measure was necessary at this time. We have not heard very much since Friday morning, other than what has been happening for the preceding two or three weeks or even for a long period. Yet, suddenly this very severe measure is introduced. I should like some sort of an explanation for that if anyone should care to give it.
Just lately we heard that Premier Bourassa had made another offer to the kidnappers. Apparently he has offered them immunity from punishment if they deliver the two victims unharmed. I can appreciate the sort of anguish he must have experienced in making this kind of offer because, in considering the safety of two persons, he had to yield a little to what we consider to be blackmail. I do not envy him his position. I think we should ofEer some alternative to the action the government has taken. This has already been mentioned on several occasions by members of the opposition. The War Measures Act is in force but it is not really necessary that it be in force for a period of six months or even longer.
I support the amendment moved by one of our members to the effect that the act be in force only for a period of a couple of weeks or long enough to give the government ample opportunity to bring in another statute or an amendment to the Criminal Code which would allow the government to deal effectively with the crisis which exists. I suggest that if such a statute should be brought in, it should contain a time limit just sufficient to meet this crisis situation.
It is likely that a new bill or an amendment to the Criminal Code to deal with this situation could be quite severe. We must be sure that such severe legislation would be limited only to the time of the crisis with which we are dealing. If it should be brought in, there should be an understanding that it would be reviewed within a certain period during a cooler time in our history, whenever that might be. In the circumstances, and considering all the factors involved, I consider it possible that invokement of the War Measures Act was the right thing to do because there may not have been any other way to handle the situation after the decision was suddenly made to take action. My only hope is that this exercise will lead to greater freedom rather than less freedom.
No one is very happy to see armed soldiers, guns and bullet-proof cars around our capital city, in the province

of Quebec or anywhere else for the purpose of protecting our citizens. It is an unusual sight and one that we have difficulty accepting. I hope that in a year or so this whole scene will become only a relic in the museum of Canadian history. In order to ensure that this happens one might try to determine why these problems have arisen and why the FLQ has flourished. Personally, I know a couple of reasons, but I believe we should also examine the basic discontent with our social structure and recognize that in many areas of our country, including Quebec, poverty is a very great problem. Unemployment, too, is a major problem and the economy in general is in a poor condition. The people of Quebec have had some difficulties with their language and some cultural problems. There are many other problems which have been plaguing the country. All of these have to be tackled in earnest, along with any new proposed legislation that will be brought in, if the solution to this crisis is to be of a lasting nature.

I have frequently felt that the inclination of members to play a role, and on many occasions to express hypocritical attitudes, dominated their instincts and inclination to be great Canadians. But in the last two days I have been encouraged at the ability of Members of Parliament to put aside their political

It seems to me that it takes a crisis like that which we are faced with today to bring out the best in Canadians. Perhaps as Canadians we have had it too easy. We have been willing to go along with the tide, to adopt a lax, lackadaisical attitude, to allow ourselves to be lulled into a sense of false security. I believe that the present crisis may elevate our parliamentary system to a level that is more respectable, and that will be admired more by Canadians.
I am a little at a loss, Mr. Speaker, to understand the sudden confusion and disturbance that has developed in the chamber. Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to participate in this debate, but after hearing the comments of some hon. members in this chamber I felt my position should also be put on record. My reasons for not wanting to participate in the debate were these. I felt the views of my colleagues from Quebec would have greater import and impact than mine with regard to the reason for the proclamation issued yesterday. I believe they know conditions in the province

of Quebec much better than I know them, and having listened to the comments of some hon. members I think they would agree.
Prince George-Peace River is a long way from the heart of the problem that required the Prime Minister to make the proclamation yesterday. Even though separated by distance, Mr. Speaker, we are no less sensitive than others to the anguish the FLQ has brought to the citizens of the province of Quebec. We are not faced with the physical presence of violence. We do not have to concern ourselves with the safety of our families. Our businesses and social activities have not been interrupted or challenged by terrorism.
Some hon. members who oppose the government's action suggest that the measure is too broad. They ask: What need is there for other provinces to be covered by the same legislation, when the cancer is rooted in only one province? Mr. Speaker, I feel that the federal responsibility is to all provinces, to all citizens. When we start considering legislation to ensure law and order for citizens in one section of our country, we are tending to balkanize Canada. We will not contribute to the balkanization of our country; legislation passed in this chamber is for all Canadians.
My friend opposite, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), insisted this afternoon that the government make the information that led to the proclamation yesterday available to Parliament. Surely, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend and others who advocate complete disclosure and revelation of facts must know that the divulging of those facts may be of greater value to the FLQ than to hon. members. Confidential information and discussions, even in caucus, oftentimes turn out to be the day's headlines. I am not implying, Mr. Speaker, that all members are loose of tongue. If I were a law abiding citizen who supplied information to the police or the government, I would start looking for a haven if I knew that my reports were being discussed in this chamber or in committee. Our intentions may be of the highest order, Mr. Speaker, but it does not require a high degree of intelligence to know that informants may be found when the type of information sought is known.

Mr. Speaker, anyone rising to say anything at this point, in view of the news that has reached us in the last few minutes, cannot but speak in sadness and with restraint. I assure hon. members that I shall exercise restraint and that I shall be as brief as I can. Indeed, apart from the news that brings a special sorrow to our hearts at this time, one would not want to indulge in any repetition at this stage of the debate. Neither do I think there is need for any recrimination at this time.
It is still my view that using the War Measures Act was a mistake. I shall express that by my vote on Monday. But I am prepared to admit that a verdict on that action which perhaps will be more valid than the judgments we try to make here will come later. That verdict will come when all the facts have been made public, maybe a few months from now. If at that point those facts justify the action, we who now feel otherwise will have to admit it. If at that point the action is not justified, the people of Canada will be able to express their opinion when they get the opportunity to do so.
The reason I would like to say a few words, even this late in the debate, is that the question we should now be facing is very simple: Where do we go from here? I have three brief suggestions to make.
The first relates to the question as to what we should do in view of the general feeling of repugnance regarding the use of the War Measures Act, a repugnance expressed not more forcibly by anyone else than it was yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
This evening I listened with interest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) when he suggested that because Parliament had put the War Measures Act on our statute books, it was anticipated that it would be used. I do not read our history that way. This evening I again read the statement made by the then minister of justice, Hon. Mr. Doherty, in August 1914, who when moving the bill the first time it was presented, assured Parliament that it was a temporary measure.
I also read this evening the words of Mr. St. Laurent in 1946 when we were in the process of getting rid of the proclamations under the War Measures Act. He said to this House that he hoped it would never be used again. It

October 17, 1970
Invoking of War Measures Act seems clear to me that an act that in 56 years has never been used in peacetime is the kind of act that really was not intended for such use. Even so, I confess that I am not happy about the suggestion that has been made repeatedly-indeed, some of my own colleagues have made the suggestion-that instead of dealing with this matter by the War Measures Act that we should amend the Criminal Code.
What bothers me about that is that the Criminal Code is a permanent piece of legislation. If we put into it measures strong enough to deal with a special situation, we may find ourselves with permanent law that goes beyond our concepts of civil liberties and should not be on our statute books.
I make the suggestion that maybe there is room in our statutes for a piece of legislation that could be known as a civil disturbances act. I have in mind an act something similar to the War Measures Act in that it would come into effect only on proclamation, but it would be a special piece of legislation for disturbances or difficulties inside the country. When proclaimed such an act would provide much narrower powers than the War Measures Act, in other words only those powers actually needed. I make this suggestion as one that might be considered. It was my intention to develop that more fully, but obviously at this hour of the morning one shortens his remarks.
Secondly, I feel we have to work very hard to show that in our kind of society we still think there is a better way than to use force or repression to deal with ideas that we do not like. Let it be clear that I am not confusing the FLQ with those other people in Quebec who would like to have independence. The FLQ is the violent expression of that idea. Because the two have got confused, we are in the position of trying to cope with an idea we do not like by use of force.
We have to cope with the idea of separatism or of Quebec being independent in a much better way, by a determined effort to make it clear that it is a better Canada, both for Quebec and the rest of us, if we remain united. I do not want to live in a Canada without Quebec.
I agree with the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) that what we are concerned about in this debate is not just saving Quebec but saving Canada.
[DOT] (1:00 a.m.)
I think that in order to do this we must rely, not on force, not on repression, not on laws or regulations which go beyond the concepts of civil liberty, but we have to work in all parties in Canada on the proposition I am sure all of us believe in, namely, that this Canada united is better for all of us than a Canada divided in any way whatsoever.
